candidates.title: Rising Q3 transportation costs squeeze manufacturers, reward railroads and reshape trade
candidates.excerpt: Rising fuel prices and freight rates are putting pressure on corporate supply chains, but sharply with different consequences: Higher costs for automakers, a competitive opening for railroads and an unexpected advantage for some U.S. oil refiners. Comments from seven executives at Ford (NYSE: F), Union Pacific (NYSE: UNP), XPO (NYSE: XPO) and Valero (NYSE: VLO) during the latest third-quarter earnings season show why transportation inflation is much more than who pays more for diesel. The effect also depends on how far a company ships, which transport networks it controls and whether its competitors face an even steeper freight bill. At Ford, Chief Financial Officer Sherry Ann House drew a distinction between the cost of moving vehicles and customers’ willingness to buy them. “Higher fuel prices are impacting our freight and energy costs. candidates.title: NTSB releases preliminary report on UP derailment in Kansas
candidates.excerpt: WASHINGTON — Damage was estimated at $2.4 million after 37 cars of a Union Pacific train derailed near Greensburg, Kan., on Oct. 15, according to a preliminary report from the National Transportation Safety Board. The train was westbound on UP’s Pratt Subdivision with three head-end locomotives, two midtrain distributed power units, and 171 loaded intermodal cars and auto racks when it derailed about 8:25 a.m. There were no injuries and no hazardous materials were released. Prior to the derailment, the train had been running at about 56 mph when it was stopped by a penalty brake application. After confirming that communication was intact with the DPUs and end-of-train device, and restoring brake pipe pressure, the engineer resumed the trip, but the train was stopped shortly thereafter by an emergency brake application, at which time the conductor observed the derailed cars. candidates.title: Switch installation celebrated at Pullman historic park
candidates.excerpt: CHICAGO — Visitors to the 19th-century Pullman factory complex on Chicago’s South Side frequently ask, “Where are the railcars?” The first step in eliminating that question took place when Norfolk Southern recently reinstalled a switch on an industrial lead two blocks east of the site that was once the conduit in and out of the sprawling plant. Next, a track will be relaid from there along the north side of 111th Street, now a grassy parkway, to a planned building to display vintage Pullman equipment. Norfolk Southern is contributing $250,000 to the venture. On Monday, Nov. 9, Friends of the Pullman National Historical Park staged a “Setting the Spikes” event. Local dignitaries were invited to don protective gear before bringing sledgehammers down on a track slab NS placed in a parking lot nowhere near where the real track will be constructed. candidates.title: Memphis-area town asks STB to require UP to keep NS intermodal terminal open
candidates.excerpt: WASHINGTON — The town of Rossville, Tenn., has asked the Surface Transportation Board to require Union Pacific to keep Norfolk Southern’s Memphis-area intermodal terminal open for at least five years after the merger. The UP-NS operating plan assumes UP will close the Rossville terminal in favor of its terminal across the Mississippi River in Marion, Ark. NS handles about 500 daily lifts at Rossville, a $125.6 million terminal that opened in 2012 with construction partly funded through a $52.5 million federal grant. Shifting Rossville’s containers to Marion would increase Marion truck traffic by 57% and force Memphis-area containers to cross the Mississippi by rail and return by truck, adding bridge traffic and drayage expense, the town argues in a filing with the STB. candidates.title: Maersk introduces Nicaragua customs transit surcharge
candidates.excerpt: Maersk has introduced an Internal Customs Transit Surcharge for Store Door shipments moving through ports in Nicaragua. The surcharge applies from 9 November 2026 and is set at US$75 per container. It will be added automatically to Maersk quotations for Store Door cargo requiring an internal customs transit declaration, known as DUCA-T. Maersk said the charge covers the use of specialised customs personnel to process transit declarations and coordinate clearance with port authorities and logistics providers. Additional port services subject to separate charges Inspections, warehousing, port fumigation and other third-party services may be invoiced separately through CAI, PAE or PAI surcharge codes. A financial fee of 3% will also apply to payments made by Maersk to third-party service providers on behalf of customers. The carrier said the new customs arrangement is intended to support timely clearance and cargo delivery while ensuring compliance with local requirements.

candidates.title: Maersk boxship knocks down crane at Yantian
candidates.excerpt: Maersk boxship knocks down crane at Yantian A Maersk-operated containership has brought down a ship-to-shore crane at China’s Yantian port after striking the structure while berthing. The incident involved the 366-m-long, 15,516 teu Maersk Cincinnati, which hit the crane at berth 12 of the Shenzhen terminal at around noon local time on November 9. Images and videos shared across Chinese social media show the crane collapsed towards the container yard, with sections of the structure lying alongside the vessel. The extent of the damage remains unclear, with no confirmed reports of injuries or details of any disruption to terminal operations. The Singapore-flagged, 2024-built boxship was operating voyage 645W on the Gemini Cooperation’s Asia-North Europe NE3 service. AIS data placed the vessel at Yantian on Monday, with the ship still alongside on Tuesday. candidates.title: AAR Reports Weekly Rail Traffic for the Week Ending October 31, 2026
candidates.excerpt: The Association of American Railroads (AAR) reported U.S. rail traffic for the week ending October 31, 2026. For this week, total U.S. weekly rail traffic was 514,080 carloads and intermodal units, up 3.5 percent compared with the same week last year. Total carloads for the week ending October 31 were 233,816 carloads, up 3.0 percent compared with the same week in 2025, while U.S. weekly intermodal volume was 280,264 containers and trailers, up 3.9 percent compared to 2025. Seven of the 10 carload commodity groups posted an increase compared with the same week in 2025. They included metallic ores and metals, up 3,883 carloads, to 25,059; chemicals, up 2,542 carloads, to 34,523; and motor vehicles and parts, up 1,351 carloads, to 16,268. Commodity groups that posted decreases compared with the same week in 2025 were grain, down 2,092 carloads, to 23,078; miscellaneous carloads, down 1,162 carloads, to 8,369; and coal, down 224 carloads, to 55,042.
